newsitem.title: UK: Inflation report knocks sterling off 2-1/2 yr high.
newsitem.headline: Inflation report knocks sterling off 2-1/2 yr high.

text.p: A hawkish Bank of England inflation report on Wednesday shocked economists and knocked the stuffing out of sterling, fresh from a trip to two-and-a-half year highs.

The pound had already slipped from its early peak of 2.5137 marks, but the Bank's assertion that another rate rise would probably be needed because the the government was unlikely to meet its inflation goal punched the unit back below 2.4900.

"To an extent it's a knee-jerk reaction. What really matters for sterling is the outlook for interest rates relative to the rest of the world," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
Analysts expressed surprise at the Bank of England's tough line, coming as it did just one week after Britain unexpectedly raised official interest rates by a quarter-point.

The Bank said the short-run rise in inflation reduced the chance of bringing it below the government's target of 2.5 percent in 1997. Inflation could rise above three percent in the next month or so, BoE chief economist Mervyn King said.
The central bank also raised eyebrows with its contention that sterling's current strength is likely to remain temporary and has no implications for inflation in the medium term.

King said the pound's rise is no substitute for higher interest rates, implicitly rejecting the old rule of thumb that a four-percent sterling appreciation has the same impact as a one-point monetary tightening.

Stuart Weatherby, UK economist at Panmure Gordon, said sterling had reacted badly to the suggestion that inflation was set to go higher. "But I wouldn't see this as a major setback for the currency market," he said.
"I think the BoE's trying to put pressure on the Chancellor and if anything, inflation towards the end of the year may start going better, given the sterling strength we've seen," he added.

But the prospect of fresh conflict between the Bank of England and the Treasury, which was apparently soothed last week when Chancellor Kenneth Clarke finally heeded Bank governor Eddie George's calls for higher rates, is bad for the pound and had helped spark sterling sales, analysts said.
"A Bank-Treasury split is a negative," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas in Paris. "It looked like they had reached a truce, but it has lasted only a week."

Sterling was quoted at 2.4880 marks by 1353 GMT, down from late Tuesday's European level of 2.5029 and over two pfennigs below its session high. Dollar/mark's retreat after rallying on the U.S. election results did the pound no favours.
Against the dollar, sterling fell to $1.6397 from the previous European close of $1.6450.

Some analysts had begun the day talking of a push through 2.52 marks to open at 2.53, with an eventual target of 2.60. But while the pound's price action after the BoE report appeared to drive that move off the agenda, most remained upbeat.

"A reminder that the UK is in a tightening cycle should make for a positive medium-term backdrop to the pound. 2.55 marks is still favoured soon," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America in London.
